Now analyse your completed table. Read down the "crops" column and then down the "dishes" column, and
look for a relationship between the two.
The relationship is hard to miss. Punjab grows wheat, and Punjabi food is built on wheat.
Karnataka grows ragi, and ragi appears in Karnataka's everyday meals. Manipur grows
rice and bamboo, and both turn up on the Manipuri plate.
This makes sense once you think about where food has to travel from. For most Of human
history, and for most families even today, the cheapest and freshest food is the food grown
nearby. A cuisine is, in large part, a set of clever answers to the question: what can we cook
And what grows here depends on two things a farmer cannot choose — the soil and the
climate. Rice needs standing water and warmth. Ragi tolerates poor soil and low rainfall.
Mustard grows in cool northern winters. India has an unusual range of soils and climates,
which is exactly why it has an unusual range of food.
Soil and climate are not the whole story. Culture, religion and history all shape what a
community eats and what it avoids. Two families in the same street, growing food from the
same fields, may cook very differently.
so regional food is explained by cultivation, and then modified by taste, culture and tradition.
